# CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR.
<sig>Dd</sig>

3222. Furthermore, loves and their affections are represented by flames, and this with an inexpressible variety. Truths, however, are represented by lights and by the innumerable modifications of light. From this, it can be evident why, in the Word, goods which belong to love are signified by flames, and truths which belong to faith are signified by lights.

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for the things that are within him. The things that are there, even if they do not appear to belong to that light, still do so, for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form derived from the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and space, which occupy the natural man to such an extent that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and attributes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he has only a perception of those things that belong to the light of the world, and not of those that belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This light, namely the light of heaven, is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. What appears as a single ray in the light of the world consists of myriads in the light of heaven. Intelligence and wisdom exist within that light. It is that light which flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, there would be no perception for man at all, for it is from that source that the things of the light of the world have life. There is a correspondence between those lights—or between those things that are in the light of heaven and those in the light of the world—when the external or natural man acts as one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of the things that are in the light of heaven.

3224. It is remarkable that man does not yet know that his intellectual mind is in a certain light which is entirely different from the light of the world. But such is the condition that, for those who are in the light of the world, the light of heaven is like darkness; and for those who are in the light of heaven, the light of the world is like darkness. This comes primarily from the loves which are the heats of light. Those who are in the loves of self and the world—that is, in the heat of the light of the world alone—are affected only by evils and falsities, and these are what extinguish the truths that are of the light of heaven. But those who are in love to the Lord and love toward the neighbor

<summary>Swedenborg distinguishes between the light of the world (natural) and the light of heaven (spiritual), explaining that human perception relies on the inflow of celestial light into the natural mind to produce intellect and wisdom.</summary>
